MetaCheck Report

epymorph turns spatial epidemic model comparisons into controlled forecasting experiments

2026-11-25 · Metacheck 0.4.4.40 · DOI 10.64898/2026.10.26.26366544

1to fix4to check0to decide by hand0fine11not applicable

To fix (1)

To fix Data Check

What we found

  • We found 2 keys (such as an API key or an access token) in 1 file. Anyone who downloads this file can use the service at the authors’ cost.
  • We classified 400 files: 49 data, 270 code, 45 documentation, 3 materials, 28 output, 5 unknown.
  • We found 26 tabular data files and extracted 345 columns from 24 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex2), plus 4 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 2 files read as a table but are not a usable rectangular dataset (pubmed-abstracts.txt: 100% of columns are free text, not variables; recall-nearmiss.csv: the file has no data rows or columns). No columns were extracted and they were not sent to the LLM. Share the underlying data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook: pubmed-abstracts.txt, recall-nearmiss.csv. We ran automated data-quality checks on 345 columns; 50 columns have at least one potential issue (19 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 12 columns with inconsistent category casing; 8 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 8 columns with numeric values stored as text; 3 columns of free text that may contain personal detail; 1 column whose values look like personal information; 1 column with leading/trailing whitespace). We detected demographic column for Age. 1 of 1 spreadsheet file has at least one formatting issue (colour coding, merged cells, empty rows/columns, or an offset header).
Show details

This module classifies repository files and, for tabular data files available locally, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

Keys in the repository

We found 2 keys (such as an API key or an access token) in 1 file. Anyone who downloads this file can use the service at the authors’ cost.

File Where Key Type of key Beginning
tests/slow/adrio/cassettes/commuting_flows_test/test_commuters_values.yaml.gz/test_commuters_values.yaml line 11640 1 brave-search-api-key BSA0V…
tests/slow/adrio/cassettes/commuting_flows_test/test_commuters_values.yaml.gz/test_commuters_values.yaml line 79578 2 brave-search-api-key BSARi…

Revoke each key with its provider and make a new one, then remove it from the files. Deleting the file or the line does not remove the key: GitHub keeps every earlier version of a repository, and the OSF keeps earlier versions of a file. Metacheck shows only the beginning of each key, and does not test whether it still works.

odin/dust/mcstate Multiple inference families behind one interface
Four methods, one family. mcstate provides a particle filter, pMCMC, SMC^2 and (added in version 2) the IF2 iterated-filtering algorithm – all built on the particle filter, all behind one interface. Nothing outside sequential Monte Carlo: no ensemble Kalman filter, no ABC, no variational family. 012-224-870-328-762 Bayesian Analysis of Nonclinical Studies to Inform Regimen Selection for Tuberculosis NA 2026 conference proceedings article Bayesian Analysis of Nonclinical Studies to Inform Regimen Selection for Tuberculosis International Society of Pharmacometrics James Clary; Shayne Watson; Khisi Mdluli; Micha Levi; Debra Flood; David Hermann; Alexander Berg <p xmlns:xsi=““http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance”” dir=““auto”” id=““d626261e101”“> Objectives: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading cause of infectious-disease related mortality worldwide. To address this critical global health challenge, new and novel shorter-duration treatment regimens must be identified. Evaluation using relevant animal models of TB such as the relapsing mouse model (RMM) is an important step in prioritizing regimens for potential clinical utility. To appropriately compare regimen performance in the RMM, incorporation of prior data and information across studies is important. The objective of this work was to improve upon our previous model-based methodology [ <a class=””xref-link”” href=””#r1””>1] by adopting a Bayesian estimation approach that incorporates prior information, adjusts for influential study-level covariates and quantifies inter-study variability to generate robust estimates of regimen efficacy to guide regimen prioritization. <p xmlns:xsi=”“http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance”” dir=““auto”” id=““d626261e109”“> Methods: Individual (mouse) level relapse events from multiple RMM studies were combined in a comprehensive dataset including relevant study level covariates for analysis. The pooled dataset was analyzed using the Bayesian modeling software, Stan (as implemented via Rstan), to obtain model-based estimates describing regimen-specific relapse probabilities at each treatment duration. The resulting parameters were used to generate cure probability vs. treatment duration profiles for all regimens in the dataset and derive metrics of interest such as time to 95% cure probability (T95). <p xmlns:xsi=”“http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance”” dir=““auto”” id=““d626261e114”“> Results: An inverse Emax (Hill) model sufficiently described the relapse probability vs. treatment duration profiles for all regimens included in the analysis. Due to differences in dosing and data availability, several related regimens (i.e., similar dosing / components) were combined which improved model stability. Credible intervals for T95, adjusted for relevant study-level covariates including mycobacterial inoculum, were obtained from the final model for comparison and relative rank-ordering assessment for regimens of interest. <p xmlns:xsi=”“http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance”” dir=““auto”” id=““d626261e119”“> Conclusions: A Bayesian modeling approach was applied for analysis of RMM study data, which improved upon the mixed-effects logistic regression model previously reported1 in both performance and flexibility in incorporation of prior information. Importantly, this serves as a framework from which performance metrics may be obtained for new and novel anti-TB regimens in the context of regimens with existing data, even in cases where within-study comparisons were not possible or historical animal-level data is not fully available. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 345 columns across 25 data files.

Issues Identified

53 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 25 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 2 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: editor settings (2). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory, .Rapp.history) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp, an interrupted save of R’s workspace, .RDataTmp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 43 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Your code was written for older versions of its packages.

  • check.py: “ModuleNotFoundError: No module named ‘numpy.lib’; ‘numpy’ is not a package”
  • analysis/manuscript_analysis/demo-covid.ipynb: “ModuleNotFoundError: No module named ‘numpy.lib’; ‘numpy’ is not a package”
  • results/demos/demo-covid.ipynb: “ModuleNotFoundError: No module named ‘numpy.lib’; ‘numpy’ is not a package”
  • analysis/manuscript_analysis/demo-flu.ipynb: “ModuleNotFoundError: No module named ‘numpy.lib’; ‘numpy’ is not a package”
  • results/demos/demo-flu.ipynb: “ModuleNotFoundError: No module named ‘numpy.lib’; ‘numpy’ is not a package”

A function or option has changed since you wrote the code, so it stops with today’s version of the package.

  1. In R, run renv::init() in your project and add the renv.lock file this creates to the deposit; in Python, run pip freeze > requirements.txt and add that file.
  2. State your version of R or Python in the README.
  3. Better still, update the code so it also works with current versions.

A script starts a program outside R or Python.

  • build_docx.py starts pandoc.

The computer we run the code on does not have this program, so we could not check these scripts; this need not be a fault of the code. Name the program, its version and where to get it in the README. A Docker image can include it.

Of 6 scripts: 0 ran without error, 6 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt).

Dependencies were installed into a throwaway library before running (pip install): 14 succeeded, 0 failed. geopandas, graphviz, humanize, joblib, matplotlib, openpyxl, pandas, Pillow, platformdirs, requests, scipy, sparklines, sympy, typing_extensions were installed.

All code and output

Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

3 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook files bundle the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the files itself, with nothing re-run. We extracted 66 result tables (305 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

The paper does not appear to report data about individual people or animals (we found: figures about groups or things), so we do not expect an ethics statement.

We based this on:

For the 2020-2021 SARS-CoV-2 winter wave, commuting data improved county-level forecasts of hospital census, yet a state-level model provided the best state-level forecasts.

For U.S.-based studies, epymorph automates the acquisition of Census population data at resolutions from state to census block group, empirical commuting flows, PRISM climate data, and CDC surveillance data, removing the requirement that users be experts in munging diverse data sources.

We find that empirical age-structured contact mixing improves influenza forecasts, increasingly so at longer horizons, whereas for SARS-CoV-2 a coarser Statelevel model outperforms county-level models at forecasting State-level data, although empirical commuting improves county-level forecasts relative to no movement.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
